messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Dancer
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Going Out: Going out, Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Avoid Therapy Content: avoid thinking about anything discussed in therapy
  Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
  Memory: Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Kofi's Story

Kofi was sixty-eight when the car hit him. He had been a dancer since he was twelve years old—first in Accra, then in London, finally in New York, where he had spent forty years teaching modern dance at a studio in Brooklyn and performing in community productions. His wife, Ama, had died three years earlier, and dancing had become even more essential to him; it was the language in which he still felt fluent, the one place where his body did not betray him. On a Tuesday afternoon in March, he was crossing Atlantic Avenue after buying groceries, the sun warm on his shoulders, thinking about the evening class he was about to teach. A delivery truck ran a red light. The impact came from his left side, a sound he could not now describe and a sensation of his ribs compressing, the world tilting, the pavement rushing toward his face.

He spent four days in the hospital. The doctors said he was fortunate—no internal bleeding, no fractures, significant bruising and soft tissue trauma but nothing that would not heal. What they did not say, and what Kofi came to believe with absolute certainty, was that his body had been fundamentally compromised. In the weeks after discharge, when he tried to return to teaching, his movements felt foreign to him, as though he were operating a machine he no longer understood. His knees buckled unexpectedly. His balance, which had been perfect for fifty-six years, now felt precarious. He could no longer trust his own body to do what he commanded it to do. This distrust extended into every corner of his life. If his body could fail him so catastrophically on an ordinary afternoon, how could he trust his judgment about anything else? He began to doubt whether he was making the right decisions, whether his perceptions of situations were sound. He could not trust that he would do the right thing anymore.

The memories of the collision itself were fragmented and incomplete. Kofi could recall the sun and the grocery bags—one had split, apples rolling across the street—but the moment of impact remained opaque, as though a section of film had been cut out. When he tried deliberately to reconstruct what had happened, to piece together a coherent story, the effort felt like pushing against a locked door. His mind would seize up. The harder he tried to remember, the more the fragments scattered. He would lie awake at night attempting to assemble a narrative of those seconds, but the gaps terrified him more than the fragments did. Not knowing what he had not seen, what he had missed, what might have happened in those missing moments—it made him feel vulnerable in a way he could not articulate. Because the memory was so fractured and incomplete, he found himself unable to predict danger. If he could not remember what had happened, how could he protect himself from it happening again? The fragmentation of his memory seemed to confirm his deepest fear: that the world was fundamentally unpredictable and that he was powerless within it.

This fear manifested as an acute hypervigilance that governed every moment outside his apartment. Kofi felt unsafe unless his back was against a wall where he could see the room. In his kitchen, he repositioned himself constantly, turning to face the window, then the doorway, then back again. When he went to the grocery store—and he went as infrequently as possible now—he would stand with his cart against a shelf, scanning the aisles, his shoulders rigid. He was on high alert when he heard unexpected or loud sounds; a car horn from the street below would send a jolt through his chest. When something took longer than expected, he assumed something bad was happening. A delayed text from his daughter made him certain she had been in an accident. A longer-than-usual wait at the pharmacy meant the pharmacist had discovered something wrong with his prescription, some institutional failure that would harm him. These interpretations felt less like thoughts and more like facts, immediate and undeniable.

The threat he felt everywhere made it impossible to go out. What had once been a simple errand—walking to the bodega, catching the bus to the studio—became a gauntlet of danger. He began to avoid going out altogether, or when he did venture out, he moved quickly and rigidly, his jaw clenched, his mind cataloguing exits. He stopped answering calls from friends and former students. Seeing people he had socialized with before the event became intolerable; they would ask how he was, and he could not bear to explain, could not find the words for how fundamentally altered he was. So he avoided them. He also avoided thinking about anything discussed in therapy—the accident itself, the specifics of his fears—because engaging with those thoughts felt like stepping into the path of the truck all over again. His world contracted week by week. He stopped teaching. He stopped going to the studio. He stopped going out except for the bare necessities, and even those trips left him trembling and exhausted.

Kofi came to see his therapist because his daughter had insisted, threatening to move back in with him if he did not get help. What frightened him most now was not the memory of the collision itself—that remained mercifully inaccessible—but the possibility that he would spend the rest of his life imprisoned by his own vigilance, his body a cage, his mind a locked room where the truth of what happened would never be fully recovered. He was sixty-eight years old and had lost the only language he had ever truly spoken.
